title: Oracy in Practice: Creating an Oracy-Rich Curriculum by Harnessing Everyday Routines essing-everyday-routines/
author: Tom Sherrington
summary: Tom Sherrington argues that an oracy curriculum does not require new programmes but can be built from everyday classroom routines teachers already use, once they are viewed through an oracy lens. He begins with conditions and values, saying teachers must explicitly value talk and give every student a voice, because oracy cannot be developed by accident. He sets aside debates and presentations as occasional enrichment and focuses on the daily routines of building knowledge. He then walks through core WalkThrus techniques, cold calling, think pair share, show-me boards, practise explaining, class discussion and elaborative interrogation, and shows which step in each amplifies oracy, such as following up every answer in cold calling or asking students to add, build or challenge in discussion. His conclusion is that these techniques are justified on cognitive science grounds alone, but an oracy orientation makes the knowledge acquisition deeper and involves every student.
points: Oracy has to be intentional: teachers need to value talk in learning and give every student a voice rather than letting the confident dominate.
Cold calling gains oracy value from Step 4, a follow-up question to every answer, which turns it into short dialogues and models listening.
Pair talk needs questions with substance and resources to think with, since thinking is only possible with knowledge.
Practise explaining and elaborative interrogation weave encoding, retrieval and generative learning together while surfacing misconceptions for the teacher.
Start with pairs and build to whole-class discussion, using scaffolds like add, build or challenge, because mechanical dialogue is a stepping stone.
quotes: You can't develop or harness oracy by accident; it needs to be intentional.
Why should a student have to compete for air time in a lesson? Why should the dominant students always dominate?
Across all subjects, students can learn through talk every lesson every day, and, in so doing, can learn to talk more effectively for different purposes.
When Step 4 becomes routine, the depth of dialogue across a class is so much deeper. In fact, CC without Step 4 is pretty shallow.
So - learning through talk is only likely to happen if the questions are designed to stimulate thinking; and thinking is only possible with knowledge.
Oracy mustn't lead to students simply recycling ignorance and prejudices - so routine use of practise explaining allows misconceptions and knowledge gaps to surface so the teacher and deal with them.
Mechanical dialogue is a win - it's a stepping stone without which many children never know what to say.
I would normally advice people start with pairs and build to whole class discussion: simple structures and maximum modelling.
